# Diagnosing High-RPM Suppressible Engine Knock on a DTDi Engine

When an engine knock disappears above 2,000 RPM and under light load, it fundamentally changes the diagnostic tree compared to a standard rod knock or piston slap case. A classic connecting rod bearing failure typically produces a metallic knocking that increases in amplitude with RPM and is often present regardless of throttle position due to mechanical clearance issues. The behavior you described—noise vanishing at higher speeds and only appearing under load—points toward an event driven by combustion dynamics, timing events, or specific accessory drive interactions rather than simple mechanical wear.

The most probable culprit on a 2004 Ford Focus 1.8TDi (74kW) is diesel particulate filter (DPF) regeneration activity or injector timing under load. Modern diesel engines rely heavily on precise fuel injection maps to manage emissions and thermal efficiency. If the ECU attempts to hold an exhaust temperature target during deceleration or light cruising, it may inject a "dieseling" dose of fuel while the throttle is closed or partially open. This can cause unburnt fuel to ignite late in the cycle against rising cylinder pressure, creating a sharp, metallic knock that sounds distinct from the engine's base firing order.

You noted the noise originates from the accessory belt side but persists with the belt removed. This observation rules out pulley bearings and tensioner failure immediately. However, it does not rule out timing chain issues entirely, though the description of "two pieces of metal knocking" rather than a rattle makes a stretched chain less likely. A worn tensioner roller on the camshaft sprocket can sometimes produce a rhythmic click that mimics metal-on-metal contact. On this specific engine architecture, the variable geometry turbine (VGT) actuator is located near the accessory drive area. If the VGT mechanism is binding or the hydraulic solenoid is stuck, it can create a distinct ticking or knocking noise under load when the turbo boost pressure fluctuates rapidly to maintain desired torque.

Another possibility involves the high-pressure fuel pump or injectors themselves. While bad injectors often cause misfires and error codes, early-stage injector nozzle issues can alter the shape of the combustion event without triggering a fault light immediately. If an injector is dripping slightly late in the compression stroke under load, the resulting afterburn creates a percussive sound that ceases when the engine hits higher RPMs because the combustion cycle shortens relative to the knock frequency threshold.

To isolate the issue without disassembly, listen carefully for the correlation between boost pressure and the noise onset. If the knock coincides exactly with turbo spool or VGT movement, focus your inspection on the variable geometry housing and its linkage. If the noise persists only when the pedal is pressed (load) but not during coast-down, this strongly suggests a combustion-related event rather than an accessory drive issue.

If you proceed to inspect the engine internals, ensure the oil system has been drained and refreshed before reassembly if any timing components are removed. Contamination from worn bearings can quickly spread through the oil gallery. Additionally, verify the camshaft position sensor alignment; incorrect timing can cause valve-to-piston interference or abnormal combustion pressures that manifest as knocking noises under specific load conditions.

For those looking to validate engine health data programmatically, tools like OBD-II scanners capable of reading live fuel injection pulse widths and exhaust gas temperature (EGT) values are essential. Correlating the RPM where the noise disappears with the EGT target curves in your scanner software can confirm whether the ECU is actively engaging a regeneration cycle or holding boost at a threshold that triggers abnormal combustion events.
